title: Short Communication In-situ grown nanoporous Zn-Cu catalysts on brass foils for enhanced electro- chemical reduction of carbon dioxide
abstract: In-situ grown nanoporous Zn-Cu catalysts were prepared by simply annealing a commercial brass foil at 500 C in air, followed by electrochemical reduction. During the annealing process, Zn preferentially melted and migrated out of the framework of the alloy to form a thin layer of ZnO on its surface. Subsequent electroreduction created nanoporous Zn-enriched surface. The Zn concentration increased from 36% to 50% by 10 min, to 81% by 3 h, and to 87% by 12 h annealing treatment while the average pore size decreased from 290 nm to 120 nm as the annealing time increased from 1 h to 12 h. Faradaic efficiency of CO2 reduction to CO and HCOOH was enhanced by nearly 4 and 6 times, respectively, as compared to untreated brass foils. The nanoporous Zn-Cu catalyst presented a stable ratio of CO/H2 and a steady working current density in a continuous electrolysis of 18 h in 0.5 M KHCO3 solution.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Global warming caused by increased CO2 concentrations in atmosphere mainly because of overuse of fossil fuels has spawned the development of CO2 conversion to fuels and chemicals powered by clean and renewable energy (solar, wind, and hydropower) [1]. CO2 electroreduction (CO2ER) at ambient pressure and temperature is one of the most promising ways for carbon balance and renewable energy storage, which has attracted worldwide interest due to its potential environmental and economic benefits [1-4]. Electrocatalysts are critical to the performance of CO2ER [5, 6] and Cu, Zn and their alloys have been intensively investigated as electrocatalyst to catalyze the CO2ER process due to their relatively high abundance, moderate catalytic activities and low cost [7-11]. Cu-Zn alloys enhance the performance of CO2ER towards reduction efficiency and selectivity as compared to their single metal Cu or Zn. However, the surface modification (e.g. morphology, composition, structure, and crystal size) of the alloy catalysts is critical. For instance, Ren et. al [12] observed that the selectivity of ethanol production vs. ethylene could be tuned by varying Zn concentration of the Cu-Zn composite oxide catalyst. Yin et. al [13] prepared Cu-Zn alloy using a vacuum sealing method, in which vaporized Zn reacted with Cu to form Cu-Zn alloy and the Zn concentration (Zn/Cu ratio) can be controlled by tuning Zn vapour pressure and heating temperature. Furthermore, porous nanostructures and stability of the catalysts are important features for the performance of CO2ER [10, 14, 15]. In general, the procedure for preparing such Cu-Zn alloy catalysts reported in literature so far is tedious and complicated while the stability of such featured electrocatalyst is of great concern [12, 13], limiting its potential for large-scale applications.
The annealing treatment has been proven highly efficient to modify the surface characteristics of Cu and Zn metals, thus improving efficiency, selectivity and stability
for CO2ER [6, 7]. Annealing Cu-Zn alloys brass in air at 300-600 C produced ZnO-CuO nanostructures with Zn enrichment for field emitter [16, 17] while heating
brass at 500-900 C in Ar/O2 (4% O2) generated one-dimensional ZnO nanostructures as an ideal field emitter [18]. Under the heating temperatures of near to the melting point of Zn, Zn phase in the brass segregated and migrated out from the framework of the alloy to its surface where Zn was oxidized by oxygen. This approach for preparing ZnO nanostructures from brass foils allows for a direct and large-area growth of ZnO nanostructures at a low cost and high efficiency. Recently, Chou et al. [19] have
successfully employed this approach by heating Cu0.8Zn0.2 at 500 C to prepare ZnO-CuO catalysts for photodegradation of organic pollutants in water. For CO2 electroreduction, nanostructural properties of metallic Zn and Cu are important [7, 10, 20]. In this study, we prepared nanostructured Zn-Cu alloy catalysts by heating
commercial Cu-Zn alloy brass foils in air at a temperature of 500 C for different times (from 10 min to 12 h), and then electrochemically reduced the oxidized brass foils for enhancing the catalytic performance for CO2 electroreduction.

sections.heading: 2.1. Chemicals
sections.text: Brass foil (h62, Cu 63% and Zn 36%, thickness 0.5 mm) was purchased from Guangdong Hong Wang Mould Co. Ltd., China. Cu foil (Alfa Aesar, thickness 0.5 mm, ˃99.999%) and Zn foil (Alfa Aesar, thickness 0.5 mm, ˃ 99.999%) were purchased from Inno-Chem Technology Co. Ltd., China. KHCO3 (99.95%) was purchased from Sigma Aldrich. The purity of CO2 gas was equal or greater than 99.99%. All the materials were used without further purification.

sections.heading: 2.2. Electrode preparation
sections.text: A brass foil (25 mm  30 mm  0.5 mm) was annealed in a tube furnace at 500 °C with an air flow at a flow rate of 300 mL/min. The annealing time was set for 1 h, unless otherwise specified. After the annealing, the brass foil was electrochemically reduced at -1.3 V versus the saturated calomel electrode (vs. SCE) in 0.5 M KHCO3 solution until the current became stable. Then, the reduced brass foil was rinsed with deionized water prior to CO2 electroreduction or soaked in acetone for storage. The prepared material was termed as nanoporous Zn-Cu bimetals (npZn-Cu). For comparison, commercial Cu and Zn foils were also annealed at 500 °C and 300 °C, and then electrochemically reduced (termed as ar-Cu and ar-Zn, respectively). The annealing temperature of 300 °C was employed for commercial Zn foils because of its melting point of 419 °C.

sections.heading: 2.3. Characterization
sections.text:
The crystalline phases of the prepared samples were investigated by an X-ray
diffractometer (XRD, Cu Kα radiation) with a scan rate of 5° min -1 in the 2θ range of 10-90°. The morphology of the prepared npZn-Cu was detected by a scanning electron microscope (SEM, JSM-6701F) equipped with an energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS, ixef). The average pore size was calculated by “Nano Measurer” software from SEM image.

sections.heading: 2.4. CO2 electrolysis
sections.text:
CO2ER was carried out in a two-compartment electrolysis cell in a plate-and-frame
shape, which was made from plexiglass and fitted with silicone pad. An anion exchange membrane (Selemion AMV, AGC Inc.) was used to separate the anodic and cathodic compartments. The prepared electrodes, RuO2/Ti, SCE and CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 solution (pH=7.2) were used as working electrode, counter electrode, reference electrode and electrolyte, respectively. The plate-and- frame electrolysis cell takes
advantages of a high electrode area (25 mm  30 mm) with respect to small electrolyte volume (18 ml), which facilitate the accumulation of the products concentration even at a low overpotential. The electrolyte was saturated with CO2 at a flow rate of 30 sccm for at least 30 min before each electrolysis and maintained during the whole electrolysis process. The potential was controlled using electrochemical workstation (CH instrument 660E, chenhua, China) with 85% IR compensation against the SCE and converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) according to: E (vs. RHE) = E (vs. SCE) + 0.0591 × pH + 0.24. Solution-phase and gas-phase products were quantified by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) and gas chromatography (GC), respectively.

sections.heading: 3. Results and Discussion
sections.text:
Fig. 1a illustrates a schematic process of npZn-Cu catalyst preparation from commercial Cu-Zn alloy brass foil by annealing and subsequent electroreduction. The SEM images and XRD patterns of a commercial brass (H62) foil corresponding to Fig.
1a are shown in Fig. 1b and c, respectively. Clearly, the annealing treatment at 500 C for 1 h produced a rough and non-porous surface with particles of 200-400 nm for brass foil while the electroreduction reduced the particle size to 100-300 nm and created abundant pores on the surface (Fig. 1b). By contrast, such a relatively uniform and porous structural surface was not obtained by the identical procedure for pure Cu or Zn foils [7, 21]. The XRD results demonstrated the removal of CuZn and the formation of ZnO by the annealing treatment as well as the generation of Zn by the subsequent electroreduction (Fig. 1c). Interestingly, Cu oxides (Cu2O and CuO) were not produced by annealing brass foil whereas Cu oxides nanoparticles were observed for pure Cu foils under similar annealing conditions [21]. Therefore, these unique features (i.e. uniform and nanoporous structure and Zn-enriched surface) of the resultant catalyst material from the commercial brass must be related to the Cu-Zn alloyed phases in the
H62 brass consisting of two alloyed phases  (Cu0.64Zn0.36) and  (CuZn). Zn was released from both the  and  phases by thermal treatment at 500 C. Then, Zn dissolved and migrated out to the surface of the alloy where Zn was oxidized by air to form ZnO. Therefore, the Cu0.64Zn0.36 phase provided a uniform framework to support the npZn-Cu composite. By contrast, the annealing treatment of the Cu-Zn alloy prepared by electrochemical deposition of Zn on the surface of pure Cu foils did not exhibited such morphology and structure [22].
Annealing time is an important parameter to affect surface characteristics of the brass
foil. The effect of annealing time from 10 min to 12 h at 500 C is shown in Fig. 2. Clearly, increasing annealing time enhanced the surface Zn concentration (see Fig. 2a EDS mappings and Fig. 2b) and reduced the surface pore size (see Fig. 2a SEM images and Fig. 2c). Longer annealing time allowed for more Zn migration and re-distribution, leading to enriched Zn on the surface. The Zn concentration increased dramatically from 36% to 81% by annealing for 3 h and reached an almost constant concentration of 87% after 6 h annealing. The average pore size decreased from 290 nm by 1 h annealing to 170 nm by 3 h and then slowly to 120 nm by 12 h. Overall, the above results demonstrated that annealing and electroreduction of commercial Cu-Zn alloy brass provided a simple and straightforward approach for preparing nanoporous Cu-Zn alloys
with enriched Zn on the surface. Specific surface area, element distribution and composition, quantities of crystals and lattice boundary are all important aspects for electrochemically catalyzed reduction of CO2 [6, 15, 21]. Therefore, the npZn-Cu prepared in this work from brass foils could be a good catalyst candidate for CO2ER.
A comparison of CO2ER performance by Cu, Zn, brass and npZn-Cu is shown in Fig. 3a. The electrolysis products by Cu and Zn were H2 (92.3%), CO (2.1%) and HCOOH (5.1%) and H2 (51.8%), CO (34.6%) and HCOOH (13.0%), respectively. Although it has higher CO2 reduction efficiency than Cu, the Zn electrode exhibited a much lower total current density. Cu-Zn alloy is expected to be a promising catalyst for CO2ER [13, 22], but the commercial Cu-Zn alloy brass does not present satisfactory faradaic efficiency of CO2 reduction. As has been reported in the literature [6], the annealing treatment at 500 C significantly enhanced CO2ER performance for the Cu electrode. Here, we observed a significant increase in faradaic efficiency of CO and HCOOH by annealing commercial Cu foils (ar-Cu) under similar conditions. In comparison, the HCOOH efficiency was increased by twice whereas the CO efficiency was not improved by annealing commercial Zn foils (ar-Zn). Interestingly, the annealing treatment significantly enhanced the CO and HCOOH efficiencies by nearly 4 and 6 times, respectively, as compared to untreated commercial brass foil. The enhanced CO2ER performance is related to the formation of nanoporous Zn-Cu layer on the surface of brass foils and this is also supported by increasing annealing time from 10 min to 3 h to enhance the CO2ER performance (cf. Fig. 2 and Fig. 3b).
The effect of applied potential on the CO2ER performance is shown in Fig. 3c. As expected, the current density increases linearly with the potential between -0.74 V and -1.17 V (vs. RHE). Interestingly, the ratio of CO/H2 remains almost unchanged at 2:1 along with different potentials. This feature is particularly favorable in view of output variability of renewable energy as Fischer-Tropsch synthesis requires a 2:1 ratio of CO/H2. In comparison, the CO/H2 ratio catalyzed by Cu changed significantly from approximately 10:1 to 3:1 along with applied potentials between -0.7 and -1.1 V (vs. RHE) [23]. Fig. 3d shows current density and faradaic efficiency for CO and H2 production in a continuous electrolysis of 18 hours. The total current density is stable around 3.1±0.2 mA cm -2 during the entire period of 18 h electrolysis while the ratio of CO/H2 is reasonably stable at 2:1. The stability of the ZnO/Zn catalyst has been of great concern owing to the low electronegativity of Zn [8, 24] whilst the long-term stability of the npZn-Cu catalyst as observed here is probably attributed to the framework of Cu-Zn alloy phase Cu0.64Zn0.36 in brass. The morphology and surface composition (O, Cu and Zn concentration) of the npZn-Cu before and after the CO2ER electrolysis of 18 h are shown in Fig. 4. Clearly, the nanoporous structure of the catalyst was intact even after 18 h electrolysis, although the surface particle size decreased and the pore size increased (Fig. 4a and b). These changes for the surface particles and pore sizes were due to further removal of oxygen atom during the reduction electrolysis (Fig. 4c). The slight increase of Cu concentration and decrease of Zn concentration identified by EDS were likely due to increased pore diameter, probably coupled with the thinning the surface layer of Zn. The major contribution of the Cu-Zn alloy substrate was to stabilize the nanoporous Zn on the surface while the latter catalyzed the electroreduction of CO2.
By contrast, Jiang et al. [10] observed that the surface morphology of nanoporous ZnO changed completely from wurtzite to amorphous and mossy structure only after electrolysis for 30 min. They prepared nanoporous ZnO by a tedious and complicated procedure (using mixture solution of zinc acetate dehydrate, urea and sodium dodecyl
sulfate by hydrothermal treatment in autoclave at 100 C for 12 h followed by thermal
decomposition at 500 C for 2 h) and increased CO faradaic efficiency by 69% as compared to commercial Zn foil. They speculated that in-situ reduction of nanoporous ZnO efficiently catalyzed CO2 electroreduction under the electrolysis condition.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text: A highly efficient and stable npZn-Cu catalyst for carbon dioxide electroreduction was prepared from a commercial Cu-Zn alloy brass H62 by a simple annealing treatment, followed by electroreduction. The enhancement of CO2 reduction performance was due to the formation of highly active ZnO/Zn enriched nanoparticles and nanoporous structure on highly stable framework of Cu0.64Zn0.36 substrate. This study demonstrates that annealing treatment provides a simple, straightforward approach to efficiently tune surface characteristics of transition metal alloys, particularly for metals with a large difference in melting point and electronegativity (e.g. Cu-Zn, Cu-Sn) for electroreduction of carbon dioxide.
